pipeline.attack_summary: The Slingshot APT uses compromised Mikrotik routers as an initial access vector, leveraging Winbox Loader to download malicious DLLs like ipv4.dll which then connect to hardcoded IPs to download additional components. The malware employs kernel-mode rootkits and vulnerable driver exploitation for persistence and privilege escalation, targeting individual users with sophisticated espionage capabilities.

indicators.context: The name appears unencrypted in some of the malicious samples – it is the name of one of the threat actor’s components, so we decided to extend it to the APT as a whole.
The initial loader replaces the victim's legitimate Windows library 'scesrv.dll' with a malicious one of exactly the same size.
One of them – ipv4.dll – has been placed by the APT with what is, in fact, a downloader for other malicious components.

When the target user runs Winbox Loader software (a utility used for Mikrotik router configuration), this connects to the router and downloads some DLLs (dynamic link libraries) from the router’s file system.
Following infection, Slingshot would load a number of modules onto the victim device, including two huge and powerful ones: Cahnadr, the kernel mode module, and GollumApp, a user mode module.
Canhadr, also known as NDriver, contains low-level routines for network, IO operations and so on.

The most sophisticated module is GollumApp. This contains nearly 1,500 user-code functions and provides most of the above described routines for persistence, file system control and C&C communications.
During our research we also found a component called KPWS that turned out to be another downloader for Slingshot components.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.

I know the Technicolor TC8717T Wireless Telephony DOCSIS 3.0 Modem, 4 Port Router which comes with ISP Xfinity, has been harnessed this attack.

The attack vector is straightforward social engineering followed by execution of a downloaded file. While some technical details about anti-analysis techniques are included, they are not part of the initial access mechanism.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with a phishing email containing a hyperlink that leads to a MediaFire download link for a 7z archive. The archive contains a new variant of NetWire RAT malware, which is executed after decompression. The malware uses anti-analysis techniques like dynamic code extraction and anti-sandboxing methods. It then establishes persistence via registry keys, collects system information, steals credentials from browsers and email clients, logs keystrokes, and communicates with a C&C server using DNS resolution to obtain the IP address. The malware is often distributed through malspam campaigns using malicious Word documents that enable macros to download GuLoader, which in turn downloads the NetWire payload.

status: experimental
description: Detects execution of the compromised SolarWinds Orion BusinessLayerHost process hosting the Sunburst backdoor, which is indicative of initial compromise via supply chain attack.
references:
    - https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/solarwinds-raindrop-malware
    - https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/12/18/analyzing-solorigate-the-compromised-dll-file-that-started-a-sophisticated-cyberattack-and-how-microsoft-defender-helps-protect/

    - https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/12/18/analyzing-solorigate-the-compromised-dll-file-that-started-a-sophisticated-cyberattack-and-how-microsoft-defender-helps-protect/

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    selection_cmdline:

    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using encoded commands
level: high

The script can be decompiled using myAut2Exe (a pre-compiled binary can be found here) after renaming the file from .au3 to .a3x. Analysis of the decompiled script shows that the sole purpose of the script is to execute a shellcode that is contained as a hex-encoded string: The screenshot above only shows an excerpt of the complete sequence to create the shellcode string. This string is then decoded to binary data and written to a newly allocated memory area using the BinaryToString and DllStructCreate function calls. Finally, two commands are executed. These commands are obfuscated as hex-encoded strings. Decoding these strings reveals their purpose, which is to make the newly allocated memory area executable with VirtualProtect and call the shellcode using CallWindowProc:

Initial analysis quickly revealed significant similarity to the DarkGate malware, based on the use of a similar initial infection routine (AutoIt scripts) and the observed C2 communication protocol, which matched past analyses of the same malware family. Further analysis confirmed this initial attribution, since embedded strings and contained functionality clearly identified the sample as part of the DarkGate malware family.
The AutoIt script is bundled with the .au3 file extension which is usually used for plain-text scripts. Instead it contains a pre-compiled script, which would typically use the .a3x extension.
The script can be decompiled using myAut2Exe (a pre-compiled binary can be found here) after renaming the file from .au3 to .a3x.
Using the Dhrake project (which uses the output generated by Interactive Delphi Reconstructor (IDR)) greatly helped to make the decompiled sample more readable.
When reverse engineering the sample, Ghidra initially was not able to reconstruct the used Delphi library functions and objects.

attack_vector.reasoning: The article explicitly describes the vulnerability as a path traversal bug and auth bypass in ScreenConnect that allows adversaries to create privileged accounts for remote control. The initial access is clearly described as exploiting this vulnerability without needing additional network requests or user interaction beyond the exploit itself.

pipeline.attack_summary: Adversaries are exploiting a path traversal bug and authentication bypass vulnerability in ScreenConnect (CVE-2024-1709 & CVE-2024-1708) to gain privileged access, then using this access for post-exploitation activities including deploying ransomware (LockBit), cryptocurrency miners, installing additional remote access tools like Simple Help RMM and Google Chrome Remote Desktop, downloading payloads via curl/certutil/Invoke-WebRequest, creating persistence mechanisms through scheduled tasks and WMI event consumers, clearing logs with wevtutil.exe, and attempting to evade detection by modifying Windows Defender exclusions.

title: Initial Access via Malicious SESSID Cookie in GlobalProtect Login
id: 5e8f4d0a-7c3b-4f2d-9a6e-1b8c9d0e1f2a
status: experimental
description: Detects an unauthenticated attacker sending a crafted HTTP request with a malicious SESSID cookie value to the GlobalProtect login endpoint, which triggers arbitrary file creation and subsequent command injection via the device telemetry feature.
references:
    - https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2024-3400
    - https://labs.watchtowr.com/palo-alto-putting-the-protecc-in-globalprotect-cve-2024-3400/

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1203
    - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection:
        cs-uri-stem|endswith: '/global-protect/login.esp'

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up clearly describes exploitation of a vulnerability (CVE-2023-27532) that allows unauthenticated access to port 9401, followed by SQL shell command execution which triggers PowerShell script execution. The attack chain is well-defined and the initial vector is explicitly described.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack began with exploitation of CVE-2023-27532 to gain unauthenticated access to Veeam Backup & Replication servers via port 9401, followed by execution of PowerShell scripts (POWERTRASH) that loaded DICELOADER via reflective PE injection. Persistence was established using a new tool called POWERHOLD which deployed DUBLOADER through side-loading of a malicious libcurl.dll. The threat actor conducted reconnaissance, credential theft, and lateral movement using WMI and SMB.

indicators.context: An SQL server process related to the Veeam Backup instance executed a shell command
The script contains an embedded payload that is executed through reflective PE injection. POWERTRASH is an obfuscated loader written in PowerShell that has been attributed to FIN7
An additional file called "445.ps1" was dropped and executed on the compromised Veeam backup servers
The filenames (e.g. icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1) used for these PowerShell scripts were also (notably) identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7
The filenames (e.g. icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1) used for these PowerShell scripts were also (notably) identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7
A custom PowerShell script, "gup18.ps1", was executed to set up an active foothold in the compromised machine by creating a persistence mechanism to execute DICELOADER on device startup
To resolve the list of collected IP addresses to their respective host names, a custom PowerShell script, "host_ip.ps1", was executed
The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, and one of them is gup.exe – Legitimate GUP.exe binary (part of the Notepad++ application)
The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, and one of them is gup.xml – Configuration file that’s part of the GUP application
libcurl.dll – .NET DLL file side-loaded by gup.exe
JZ4qWKZW – Encoded DICELOADER payload that’s loaded and executed by libcurl.dll
jkBDfXaL.bat – Batch file that executes gup.exe
0JNvHvAz.vbs – VBScript file that executes the batch file

The crafted loader is designed to mimic the legitimate libcurl.dll file by including export function names found in the legitimate version and thus imported by the GUP executable. Only one of the export functions, namely "curl_easy_init" contains malicious code. This unique loader has not been previously seen in FIN7’s attack arsenal, and we are now tracking it as DUBLOADER
This unique PowerShell script has not been previously seen in the attack arsenal of FIN7, and we are now tracking it as POWERHOLD
